question: What is the main thing sedative medications do to the body?
explanation: Sedatives help you relax by slowing down brain activity and calming the central nervous system. Think of it like hitting the slow-down button in your brain! [learn more](GNS223_U6_T2#GNS223_U6_T2_h1)

question: Why is keeping a close eye on a sedated patient such an important nursing duty?

options.A: The effect of sedatives exists on a sliding scale from calm to dangerous coma
options.B: Patients develop permanent neurological damage after a single dose
options.C: Medication clearance happens instantly through the skin
options.D: Sedatives consistently increase blood pressure and heart rate over time

explanation: Patients can drift easily from peaceful sleep into dangerously slow breathing. That is why watching them closely is a vital part of keeping them safe! [learn more](GNS223_U6_T2#GNS223_U6_T2_h1)

question: Which drug class is most risky for a fatal overdose because it lacks a simple reversal drug?
explanation: Barbiturates are very strong. Unlike benzodiazepines which have a handy reversal drug like flumazenil, barbiturates can easily cause fatal breathing arrest. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T2#GNS223_U6_T2_h2)

question: Why are non-benzodiazepine sleeping pills so popular for short-term insomnia?

options.A: They stimulate the central nervous system to keep patients alert during sleep
options.B: They target specific sleep receptors to induce rest with fewer daytime hangover effects
options.C: They completely eliminate the risk of developing drug tolerance
options.D: They permanently cure chronic sleep disorders after one week of use

explanation: These drugs help patients fall asleep fast and wear off quickly by morning, so they do not wake up feeling groggy. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T2#GNS223_U6_T2_h2)

question: Which main chemical messenger in the brain do most sedative drugs target to slow things down?
explanation: Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) is the body's natural brake pedal. Sedatives step on this pedal to help calm brain activity. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T2#GNS223_U6_T2_h3)

question: How do sedatives stop brain cells from firing electrical signals?

options.A: By destroying the chemical messengers before they reach neighboring cells
options.B: By opening chloride channels to make the inside of the neuron more negative
options.C: By blocking sodium channels so electrical charges leave the brain completely
options.D: By increasing the speed of calcium flow across the cellular membrane

explanation: When negative chloride ions rush inside the cell, it becomes much harder for the nerve cell to fire off an electrical signal. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T2#GNS223_U6_T2_h3)

question: Which of these is NOT a normal use for sedative medications?
explanation: Sedatives only calm the nervous system. They do not kill bacteria—that is a job for antibiotics! [learn more](GNS223_U6_T2#GNS223_U6_T2_h4)

question: An ICU patient is intubated and fighting the breathing machine. What is the doctor most likely to order?

options.A: Administering a continuous sedative infusion to calm the central nervous system
options.B: Encouraging physical exercise to tire out the skeletal muscles
options.C: Providing a strong stimulant medication to increase lung capacity
options.D: Applying topical anesthetic cream directly to the chest wall

explanation: Sedatives help keep critical care patients comfortable so they can rest easily on life support without fighting the ventilator. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T2#GNS223_U6_T2_h4)

question: Why is mixing a sedative with alcohol so dangerous?

options.A: Combining them stops the digestive tract from absorbing any nutrients
options.B: The mixture causes an immediate and permanent increase in blood pressure
options.C: Both substances depress the central nervous system and multiply each other's effects
options.D: Alcohol instantly neutralizes the sedative, causing severe toxic shock in the liver

explanation: Both alcohol and sedatives slow down brain function. Combined, they team up to dangerously depress breathing and heart rate. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T2#GNS223_U6_T2_h5)

question: An elderly patient takes a bedtime sedative. What is a key safety point for the nurse to plan for?

options.A: Restricting all fluid intake for twelve hours prior to taking the medication
options.B: Checking blood glucose levels every two hours throughout the night
options.C: Implementing strict fall precautions due to morning dizziness and slowed reflexes
options.D: Encouraging immediate morning jogging to clear the drug from the bloodstream

explanation: Older adults process these drugs more slowly, leading to morning grogginess and an increased risk of nasty slips and falls. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T2#GNS223_U6_T2_h5)

question: What does drug tolerance mean?

options.A: Having an allergic skin rash develop after starting a new prescription
options.B: The body clearing the medication from the kidneys within minutes
options.C: Experiencing severe tremors immediately after taking a single pill
options.D: Needing larger doses of a drug over time to get the same physical effect

explanation: Tolerance happens when the body gets so used to a drug that it takes a higher dose to feel the same result. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T2#GNS223_U6_T2_h6)

question: Why can stopping a long-term sedative suddenly trigger seizures?

options.A: The sudden lack of medication causes permanent damage to the heart muscle
options.B: The liver immediately releases stored toxins directly into the bloodstream
options.C: Blood pressure drops to zero because the blood vessels lose all tone
options.D: Removing the drug causes a rebound of extreme nervous system overactivity

explanation: When you take away the medication that was keeping the brain calm, the nervous system bounces back with a wild surge of activity. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T2#GNS223_U6_T2_h6)

question: Which vital sign check needs immediate nursing action after a patient takes a sedative?

options.A: Respiratory rate dropping below twelve breaths per minute
options.C: Heart rate staying steady at seventy-two beats per minute
options.D: Blood pressure reading of 120 over 80 millimeters of mercury

explanation: A slow breathing rate is a major red flag for dangerous central nervous system depression. Always watch the airway first! [learn more](GNS223_U6_T2#GNS223_U6_T2_h7)

question: A patient wakes up restless, pacing, and yelling after getting a sedative. What is this unexpected reaction called?
explanation: A paradoxical reaction is when a drug does the exact opposite of what you expect—making someone hyper instead of calm! [learn more](GNS223_U6_T2#GNS223_U6_T2_h7)
